title: Count Increasing Quadruplets
statement: The array `nums` has length n and holds every integer from 1 to n exactly once. Count the index quadruplets `(i, j, k, l)` with `0 <= i < j < k < l < n` whose values satisfy `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] < nums[l]`: the first value is the smallest, the last is the largest, and the two middle values appear in decreasing order. Return the number of such quadruplets.
constraints: All values in nums are distinct, so nums is a permutation of 1..n
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every quadruplet is O(n⁴). The pattern `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] < nums[l]` splits naturally: first find the "dip" triple `(i, j, k)` where `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]`, then any later `l` with `nums[l] > nums[j]` finishes it. If we remember, for each middle index `j`, how many dip triples end before the current position, one left-to-right sweep can both build new triples and complete old ones.

## Approach

1. Keep `triples[j]`: the number of pairs `(i, k)` seen so far with `i < j < k` and `nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]`.
2. Move `k` from left to right. For it, scan every `j < k` while counting in `smaller` how many earlier values are below `nums[k]`.
3. If `nums[j] < nums[k]`, then `k` can be the last index `l` for every triple stored at `j`: add `triples[j]` to `count`. Then `j` itself is one more smaller value, so increase `smaller`.
4. Otherwise `nums[j] > nums[k]`, and every smaller value before `j` (there are `smaller` of them) forms a new triple `(i, j, k)`: add `smaller` to `triples[j]`.
5. Return `count`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3, 2, 4, 5]`. At `k = 2` (value 2), `j = 0` gives `smaller = 1`, and `j = 1` (value 3) is bigger, so `triples[1] = 1` (the triple 1, 3, 2). At `k = 3` (value 4), `j = 1` is smaller than 4, so `count += triples[1]` gives 1. At `k = 4` (value 5) the same happens again, so `count = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): two nested loops over the indices.
- Space: O(n) for `triples`.

## Pitfalls

- Add `triples[j]` to `count` before `triples[j]` could include the current `k`; the two branches never touch the same `j` in one step, so the order is safe.
- Reset `smaller` for every `k`: it counts values below `nums[k]`, which changes with `k`.
- The answer can exceed 2³¹ for long arrays; use a 64-bit type in Java or C.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `triples[j]` | dip triples `(i, j, k)` with middle `j` found so far |
| `k` | current index: last index for old triples, third index for new ones |
| `j` | earlier index being compared with `k` |
| `smaller` | how many of `nums[0..j-1]` are below `nums[k]` |
| `count` | quadruplets found so far |
